description:
Coding the backend & modular physics engine for an interactive Moon landing simulator.
Looking for:
• 3D/Frontend Dev: WebGL, Three.js, or Unity to bring physics to life.
• Data Scientist: To fetch NASA lunar datasets.
• UI/UX & Pitcher: For dashboard design & jury presentation.
We have a massive technical advantage with a pre-built engine. Let’s win this globally! DM me to join.
summary: CLPS Lunar Mission Lite answers, in plain words, the question a CLPS mission planner or a curious student asks about a place on the Moon: will a lander there have power, can it talk to Earth, will it get through the night, and when can it get there? It compares up to three landing sites over the same days, analyses any point on the Moon hour by hour with JPL's DE440 ephemeris and NASA's LOLA terrain, simulates a lander's battery and the ground temperature, plans 2026 launch dates for every CLPS site, shows the Mons Mouton region in 3D with shadows computed from the terrain, and explains how every number was checked, including the checks that failed. Everything runs in the visitor's browser; nothing is sent to a server.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lite turns a lunar mission analysis library into pages anyone can use:

- Compare: two or three places over the same days: sunlight, longest night, coldest ground, battery needed, ground slope, Earth in view, Deep Space Network contact, longest silence, landing windows and eclipses. Each row says what it means, and the best value is marked only when the difference is larger than the method's own uncertainty.

- Pick a point: click anywhere on the Moon for six plain answers, the sky as seen from the ground (terrain horizon, the Sun's and the Earth's paths), a timeline, "Will a lander get through the night?" (ground temperature and an hour-by-hour battery simulation of your own lander), contact and landing windows, CSV downloads and a printable one-page report.

- When to launch: a 2026 calendar for every CLPS site, from 1,830 Earth-to-Moon transfers, showing the days a lander can leave and land in sunlight.

- 3D: the Mons Mouton region (IM-2 and Griffin-1) with real terrain and shadows computed on the GPU at any hour, a lander's-eye view facing the Earth or the Sun, any clicked spot's own horizon and next 30 days, a guided tour, and the Earth-to-Moon journeys of IM-1, IM-2 and our Griffin-1 forecast.

- Maps, Griffin-1 and How we know: polar maps of Earth contact, the Griffin-1 forecast we registered on 27 October 2026 before its launch, and every validation check, passed or failed, with what it means for the answers.

- Expert mode (/pro/): the full interface of the library.

HOW IT WORKS

Sun and Earth directions and the Moon's orientation come from JPL DE440 as an hourly table, worked out in the browser. Near the poles the horizon comes from NASA LOLA elevation maps (120 m), with the Moon's curvature. The ground temperature uses the regolith model of Hayne et al. (2017); the battery is simulated hour by hour. Every comparison rule, threshold and tie tolerance is written in the page next to the number.

WHAT EXISTED BEFORE THE EVENT, AND WHAT WE BUILT DURING IT

Lite is built on our own open-source library clps-lunar-browser (physics engine, data and expert interface), which existed before the event. It is pinned unchanged as a git submodule at commit 464f55c (7 November 2026). Everything outside it was built during the event on 14-15 November 2026: the Lite interface, the comparison logic, the survival check, the launch calendar, the 3D page, the report, the How we know page, the design and the tests. The commit history starts on 14 November.

A FINDING DURING THE EVENT

The 3D page traces a spot's own horizon on the 120 m terrain. It showed that the 5 km horizon grid used on the other pages puts the horizon too high on summits: at Mons Mouton the Earth is in view 83% of the next 30 days with a longest silence of 5.2 days, not 64% and 9.7 days. The 3D page shows both, and the README says so.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

For mission and payload teams scoping where and when to land, for students learning with real data, and for anyone who wants to check our Griffin-1 forecast. Once Griffin-1 lands, we will compare the real landing with what we registered and publish the result, pass or fail.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite and d3 for Lite; WebGL2 for 3D; Python with NumPy, SciPy and SpiceyPy for the library; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/dundaryusuf566-maker/clps-lunar-mission-lite (MIT). Slides (7, PDF): docs/clps-lunar-mission-lite-slides.pdf in the repository.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA polar elevation maps LDEM_75S_120M and LDEM_75N_120M (PDS). We compute the terrain horizon near both poles from them, with the Moon's curvature: when the Sun and the Earth are above the mountains and crater rims. They also give the ground slope, the polar Earth-contact maps and the 3D terrain with its computed shadows.

JPL DE440 planetary ephemeris (NAIF SPICE kernel). It gives the positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. We turned it into an hourly table for 2024-2028 that the browser reads to place the Sun and the Earth in the sky of any point on the Moon, and to design the Earth-to-Moon transfers.
NAIF lunar orientation kernel (MOON_PA frame, DE440). It gives the Moon's exact orientation, so that latitudes, longitudes and LOLA terrain line up correctly with the Sun and the Earth.

LOLA average illumination map AVGVISIB_75S_120M (Mazarico et al. 2011, NASA Goddard). We used it as an independent check of our terrain horizons: our computed share of time in sunlight around Malapert A and Mons Mouton matches NASA's map within 0.2 percentage points (median).

LRO Diviner polar cumulative temperature products (Williams et al. 2019, PDS Geosciences). We compared our ground temperature model with them at the CLPS landing points. At night and in shadow the model agrees; in sunlight near the pole it is about 30 K too cold, so this pre-registered check fails, and the site says so.
projectRefs: Our own open-source library clps-lunar-browser (https://github.com/dundaryusuf566-maker/clps-lunar-browser, MIT), written by our team before the event and pinned unchanged at commit 464f55c (7 November 2026): the physics engine, the processed data and the expert interface that Lite builds on.
